entities.summary:
Maus, a groundbreaking graphic novel created by Art Spiegelman between 1980 and 1991, stands as a pivotal work in the realm of literature and Holocaust representation. This dual narrative intertwines the harrowing experiences of Spiegelman's father, Vladek, a Polish Jew and Holocaust survivor, with the contemporary struggles of the author in understanding this traumatic legacy. Set against the backdrop of World War II, Maus employs the unique medium of comics to depict the complexities of memory, trauma, and identity, thus marking its significance in both literary and historical contexts.

The novel's publication was a watershed moment in the graphic novel genre, with its first volume, Maus I: My Father Bleeds History, released in 1986, and the concluding volume, Maus II: And Here My Troubles Began, in 1991. Spiegelman utilized anthropomorphic characters, portraying Jews as mice and Nazis as cats, to convey the stark realities of the Holocaust in a visually compelling manner. This innovative approach not only broadened the scope of graphic storytelling but also challenged prevailing narratives about the Holocaust, making the subject accessible to a wider audience. The work was met with critical acclaim, winning the Pulitzer Prize in 1992, and has since been integrated into educational curricula around the world.
